units.title: Why cache: recomputation in autoregressive decoding
outcomes: Explain why cached keys and values remove repeated projection and attention work while queries stay token-specific.
Derive naive versus cached attention work across generated tokens and name the terms that remain.
Compute the repeated-prefix share for a generation length from the triangular sum.
units.why: Serial generation reprocesses its own prefix at every step, so cost grows faster than length. The cache is the one idea that removes that repeated work, and every later unit builds on it.

next.note: Build the cache you just motivated.
See how the two phases stress hardware differently.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 21 Section 2: KV cache saves \(K\) and \(V\) only
study.locator: Section 2 through the AttentionWithKVCache class and the 5-token equivalence check (max diff 2e, cache shapes [1,4,1,8] growing to [1,4,5,8])

focus: Each new token depends on all past tokens, so naive generation reruns the full prefix. The triangular sum 1 to \(n\) is the proxy for that repeated work.
Past tokens never change, so their \(K\) and \(V\) projections stay valid. The new token still needs a fresh \(Q\) to score against cached \(K\).
The cache removes \(K\) and \(V\) recomputation and past hidden-state work. It does not remove the new \(Q\) projection or the read of cached \(K\) and \(V\).
Cached and uncached runs compute the same function. Identical outputs are the correctness check, not a coincidence.
units.reproduce: Derive the triangular naive cost \(n(n+1)/2\) for \(n\) tokens, the cached per-step new-token cost, and the 99.8 percent repeated-work share at \(n\) equal to 1000.
traps: Thinking the cache skips attention. It skips recomputing past \(K\) and \(V\), but each step still reads the full cache to score the new query.
Caching the query. Queries are token-specific, so caching them across steps is wrong; only \(K\) and \(V\) persist.
Reading speedup from multiply counts as GPU time. Counts prove the scaling change; wall time needs warmup and synchronization, which belong to the measurement unit.

selfTest.q: Why are \(K\) and \(V\) reusable across steps but \(Q\) is not?
selfTest.a: Past tokens never change, so their \(K\) and \(V\) projections stay valid. The new token needs a fresh \(Q\) to score against the cached \(K\), so \(Q\) work remains each step.

selfTest.q: Under the triangular proxy, what share of work is repeated prefix processing when generating 1000 tokens?
selfTest.a: 99.8 percent. Total proxy cost is 500500, new-token work is 1000, so 499500 of 500500 is avoidable recomputation.

selfTest.q: microkv.py asserts the cached and uncached token lists are identical. Does the cache change the sampling distribution?
selfTest.a: No. It memoizes the same math, so greedy tokens must match exactly. Logits can differ in the last bits because the cached path multiplies differently shaped tensors, so compare them with a small tolerance; a larger mismatch is a bug in positions, masking or stale state.

selfTest.q: In the Modern 21 demo with d_model 32 and 4 heads, what is the \(K\) cache shape at step 5 and what does each dim mean?
selfTest.a: [1,4,5,8]: batch 1, 4 heads, 5 cached tokens, head dim 8. Step \(i\) holds \(i\) tokens and each step computes \(K\) and \(V\) for 1 new token only.

units.title: Building a KV cache
outcomes: Implement per-layer KV allocation, append and single-token cached decode with absolute position offsets for the tiny transformer.
Explain MHA, MQA and GQA head mappings and the repeat_interleave rule for shared KV heads.
Explain KV tensor shapes and why each layer owns its cache for its own sequence.
units.why: A cache that shares layers, mixes sequences or misplaces positions returns fluent garbage with matching shapes. Ownership, layout and offsets are what make it correct.

study.locator: GroupedQueryAttention (num_kv_groups with group_size, \(K\) and \(V\) cache on dim 2, repeat_interleave mapping with the repeat versus repeat_interleave comment, q_positions versus k_positions mask) plus the README bytes formula with n_kv_heads and the 4096/32/32/32768 example

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 21 Sections 2 and 4: shapes and head sharing
study.locator: Section 2 shape evolution ([batch, num_heads, cached_seq_len, d_k] from [1,4,1,8] to [1,4,5,8]) and Section 4 MHA/MQA/GQA (32 \(Q\) heads with 32, 8 and 1 KV heads at 8K, the 8 \(Q\) with 2 KV repeat_interleave demo, savings ratio 32/8 = 4x)
study.depth: Skip Sections 5 to 8 and 10 (quantization, GGUF, PagedAttention, FlashAttention, batching) until their own units.

focus: Each layer owns its \(K\) and \(V\) tensors and each batch row owns its positions. Sharing a cache across layers or sequences mixes unrelated spaces.
Append grows the sequence dim by the new chunk only. Prefill appends the whole prompt at once, decode appends one token per step.
Positions are absolute. pos_ids and the mask pointer advance by the chunk length, so decode step \(k\) uses position current_pos plus \(k\).
GQA stores fewer KV heads and expands them with repeat_interleave. With 8 \(Q\) heads and 2 KV heads, heads 0 to 3 share KV head 0.
units.reproduce: Write the cache-owning attention forward from scratch: buffers, append, pointer-based mask slice, absolute pos_ids, reset, and the GQA repeat_interleave mapping for 8 \(Q\) heads with 2 KV heads.
traps: Forgetting reset_kv_cache between independent generations. Stale \(K\), \(V\) and pointers leak the old sequence into the new one.
Using repeat instead of repeat_interleave for grouped heads. Tiling maps the wrong KV head to each query group while shapes still match.
Restarting positions at 0 on every decode step. Absolute embeddings repeat and RoPE rotations reuse early angles, so logits diverge from the full prefix.

selfTest.q: After a 4-token prefill, the first decode step feeds 1 token. What are the \(Q\) and \(K\) lengths and which mask row applies?
selfTest.a: \(Q\) has 1 token and \(K\) has 5 (4 cached plus 1 new). The pointer is 4, so the slice is row 4 over 5 columns, which lets the new query attend to all 5 positions.

selfTest.q: With 32 \(Q\) heads and 8 KV heads, which \(Q\) heads share KV head 0, and why repeat_interleave?
selfTest.a: \(Q\) heads 0 to 3 share KV head 0 in contiguous groups of 4. repeat_interleave gives [K1,K1,K2,K2], while repeat would tile as [K1,K2,K1,K2] and map the wrong heads.

selfTest.q: Why must decode pos_ids use current_pos, and what breaks for RoPE if they restart at 0?
selfTest.a: Positions are absolute. Restarting at 0 reuses early embeddings and early RoPE angles for late tokens, so relative distances are wrong and logits diverge from the full prefix.

selfTest.q: Two layers share one cache object to save memory. What fails?
selfTest.a: Each layer has its own projections, so its \(K\) and \(V\) live in different spaces. Sharing mixes them and equivalence fails; each layer needs its own cache just as each sequence needs its own rows.

study.title: JAX scaling book inference: ragged reads and the EOS loop
study.locator: Tricks section (ragged HBM reads and Paged Attention that read only the non-padding part) and The Basics (Generation repeats until EOS or a maximum length)

focus: Generated tokens must match exactly at a fixed seed; logits must match within a small tolerance, such as 1e-5 in float32, because different matmul shapes round differently. Check both before trusting any timing.
Variable lengths need per-row lengths and padding masks. Reading the padded tail as real tokens breaks both equivalence and the batch.
Finished sequences need compaction: free or clear their rows, compact the batch, and stop them at EOS plus a length cap. Reused slots must be cleared first.
Truncation, forks and reuse without reset are stale-cache hazards. Chunked prefill and windowed caches must preserve order and positions.
units.reproduce: Write the equivalence harness: exact token match and per-step logits within tolerance for full-prefix versus token-by-token cached decoding, plus the chunked-prefill case (4-token window over 10 tokens) and the position-overflow assert case.
traps: Testing equivalence on one prompt length and head count. Offset, GQA grouping and batch bugs hide until adversarial shapes and longer contexts.
Freeing a finished row without clearing it. The next request inherits old \(K\) and \(V\) and attends to another sequence, which looks like a model bug.
Truncating the cache but keeping old position ids. Tokens shift left while positions stay high, so RoPE and absolute embeddings disagree with the full prefix.

selfTest.q: Cached and full-prefix logits differ from position 0 onward. What class of bug is it?
selfTest.a: A systematic one: wrong weights, a different prompt, a stale cache from a prior run, or a wrong mask or position base. Late-only divergence would point at windows or truncation instead.

selfTest.q: With kv_window_size 4, a 10-token prompt prefills in 3 chunks and generates 2 tokens. What total length and input check must hold?
selfTest.a: 12 total tokens. The first 10 must equal the input, as the chunking test asserts with shape 12 and input preservation.

selfTest.q: Batch lengths are [3,9,5]. Why does CS336 run attention per sequence but concatenate to [17,H] for the MLP?
selfTest.a: MLP weights are shared, so concatenated tokens batch well. Attention KV differs per sequence, so scores must stay per sequence; padding all to 9 wastes compute.

selfTest.q: A finished sequence is freed without clearing and a new request reuses the slot. What hazard and what fix?
selfTest.a: A stale-cache hazard: the new request attends to old \(K\) and \(V\), possibly leaking another sequence. Clear or reset slots on finish, compact the batch, and test slot reuse against the full prefix.

units.title: KV memory arithmetic
outcomes: Derive KV bytes per token, sequence, layer and batch from layers, KV heads, head dim, dtype and batch.

Explain the quantized-cache trade-off: a smaller cache for a small quality risk.
units.why: The cache can outweigh the weights at long context, so every serving decision starts with its size. One formula with head count and dtype predicts whether a workload fits before anything runs.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 11 Sections 1 and 2: back-of-envelope and head schemes
study.locator: Section 1 (Llama-7B 32K FP16 back-of-envelope with the cache above the 13 GB weights) and Section 2 (MHA, GQA-8, GQA-4 and MQA table at 32768 tokens with the kv_cache_elements function)

focus: Bytes equal \(\text{batch} \times \text{seq\_len} \times \text{layers} \times \text{n\_kv\_heads} \times \text{head\_dim} \times 2 \text{ for } K \text{ and } V \times \text{bytes per element}\). Every term is load-bearing.

MHA stores \(n_{\text{heads}}\) KV heads, MQA stores one, and GQA stores something in between, so the saving is \(n_{\text{heads}}/n_{\text{kv-heads}}\). In the Raschka estimator, --n_kv_groups is the number of query heads per KV head: 32 heads with --n_kv_groups 4 store 8 KV heads.
Dtype scales the total directly: FP16 2 bytes, INT8 1 byte, INT4 half a byte. Quantized cache is lossy while head sharing is structural.
The estimator divides by \(1000^3\) (GB) and the notebooks by \(1024^3\) (GiB). Same bytes, different labels.
units.reproduce: Derive per-token, per-layer and total KV bytes for Llama-7B at 32K FP16 in both GB and GiB, plus the 4-group GQA and INT8 savings, from the head formula.
traps: Forgetting one factor of 2. \(K\) and \(V\) each store a full vector, so dropping either 2 halves or doubles the answer.
Counting query heads instead of KV heads under GQA. Only KV heads occupy cache; 32 \(Q\) heads with 8 KV heads store 8, not 32.
Comparing GB and GiB numbers as if they disagree. 17179869184 bytes is both 17.18 GB and 16.0 GiB.

selfTest.q: With 32 heads and head dim 128 in FP16, what are the \(K\) plus \(V\) elements and bytes per token per layer?
selfTest.a: 8192 elements (\(32 \times 128 \times 2\)) and 16384 bytes (\(\times 2 \text{ bytes}\)), which is 16 KiB.

selfTest.q: Same model with 32 layers at 16384 tokens FP16. What is the total cache?
selfTest.a: \(4294967296 \text{ elements} \times 2 \text{ bytes} = 8589934592 \text{ bytes}\), which is 8.0 GiB in \(1024^3\) units.

selfTest.q: The estimator says 17.18 GB and notebook math says 16.0 for Llama-7B at 32K. Which is right?
selfTest.a: Both. The bytes are 17179869184 either way; the estimator divides by 1000 cubed (GB) and the notebook by 1024 cubed (GiB). State the units.

selfTest.q: 32 heads at bf16 with the estimator's --n_kv_groups 4, which stores 8 KV heads, then an INT8 cache. What are the savings?
selfTest.a: Head sharing gives 32/8 = 4x (MHA 17.18 GB to GQA 4.29 GB decimal, as run). INT8 halves it again to about 2.15 GB, for 8x versus FP16 MHA at a small quality risk.

units.title: Two regimes: prefill and decode
outcomes: Explain prefill parallelism versus decode serialization and why one is compute-bound and the other bandwidth-bound.

Explain batch effects and phase interference between concurrent prefills and decodes.
units.why: Latency and throughput numbers are meaningless without the regime behind them. Prefill scales with prompt length in parallel while decode pays per token in serial, so each needs its own bottleneck story.

next.note: Measure the two regimes you just analyzed.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 21 Section 9: prefill versus decode
study.locator: Section 9 table (prefill parallel and compute-bound with FlashAttention versus decode serial and bandwidth-bound with KV cache plus PagedAttention) with the 50-token prefill versus 20-step decode timing cell

focus: Prefill processes the whole prompt at once like training, so long prompts saturate compute. Decode handles one token per request, so it streams weights and KV from memory.
MLP intensity is \(B \times T\): batching requests helps decode. Attention intensity is about 1 at decode because each sequence owns its KV, so batching cannot fix it.
Short prefills and single-token decodes can be launch-bound: tiny kernels cost more to start than to run. Long contexts and big batches turn capacity-bound when the KV no longer fits.
A prefill running beside decodes steals the compute the decodes share. That interference is why serving separates or interleaves the phases.
units.reproduce: Derive MLP intensity \(B \times T\) and attention intensity \(S \times T/(S+T)\), then classify short prefill, long prefill, single decode and batched decode as launch, compute, memory or capacity limited.
traps: Expecting bigger batches to fix decode attention. Batching helps MLP reuse of weights, but per-sequence KV keeps attention bandwidth-bound.
Calling decode compute-bound because FLOPs look small. Small FLOPs with large streaming reads is the definition of bandwidth-bound.

Treating every small step as compute-bound. A 32-token prefill sits far below the roughly 240-token critical batch, so streaming the weights bounds it; for a tiny model, kernel-launch overhead can dominate even that.

selfTest.q: MLP intensity is \(B \times T\). Compare \(B=8\), \(T=1\) decode with \(B=1\), \(T=1024\) prefill against a critical batch near 240.
selfTest.a: 8 versus 1024. The decode step is memory-bound and the prefill is compute-bound in bf16.

selfTest.q: Attention intensity is \(S \times T/(S+T)\). Compare prefill with \(S=2048\) to decode with \(S=2048\) and \(T=1\).
selfTest.a: Prefill gives \(S/2=1024\) (compute-bound) while decode gives about 1 (always bandwidth-bound). Batching does not raise the decode value because each sequence has its own KV.

selfTest.q: The JAX Pop Quiz bounds a 30B step at 2.5 ms for batch 4 and 21 ms for batch 256. Why does latency rise while throughput improves?
selfTest.a: Batch 4 is memory-bound (batch x KV plus params over bandwidth). Batch 256 pushes the MLP into the compute-bound term, so each step costs more but carries 64x the tokens.

selfTest.q: A 32-token single-stream decode feels slow despite tiny FLOPs. Name two likely limiters besides FLOPs.
selfTest.a: Kernel-launch overhead on tiny ops and memory bandwidth from streaming weights plus KV each step. Capacity is not the issue at this size.

study.locator: main() (torch.cuda.synchronize before and after the run, time.time around 200-token generation from Hello, I am, tokens/sec plus max_memory_allocated)

study.title: CS336 Lecture 10: metrics and batch trade-offs
study.locator: landscape (TTFT, latency in seconds per token and throughput in tokens per second, training parallel versus inference sequential) and throughput_and_latency (Llama 2 13B on H100 at batch 1, 64 and 256 with smaller batches favoring latency and larger favoring throughput, TTFT as a function of prefill)

focus: TTFT comes from the prefill call plus the first sample. ITL is the mean over steady decode steps. Never average the two phases together.
Warm up first and discard the cold runs: allocation, compilation and caches make the first iteration much slower than the rest.
CUDA launches are async, so synchronize around each timed region. Without it the clock measures launch speed, not work.
Fix everything else before comparing: same prompt, batch, lengths and seeds, tokenization outside the clock, and identical outputs on both sides.
units.reproduce: Write the phase-split benchmark: warmup, synchronized prefill timing for TTFT and per-token decode timing for ITL at two context and batch regimes with identical-output checks.
traps: Timing tokenization with the model. Encode and decode outside the clock or tokenizer speed masquerades as model speed.
Claiming a speedup with different outputs. Different lengths or sampling paths do different work, so verify identical tokens first.
Reporting one blended rate. A fast prefill can hide a slow decode and misdirect the next optimization.

selfTest.q: Where do TTFT and ITL come from in the Modern 21 Section 9 cell?
selfTest.a: The cell times one 50-token prefill call (the TTFT proxy; a full TTFT adds the first sample) and takes ITL as the mean of the 20 one-token calls. Mixing them hides the regime difference.

selfTest.q: CUDA timing without synchronization shows impossibly fast decodes. Why?
selfTest.a: Kernel launches are async, so the clock measures launch instead of work. Synchronize before and after each region as the Raschka main() does.

selfTest.q: The first timed run is 3x slower than repeats. What do you do?
selfTest.a: Discard it as warmup (cold allocation, compilation and caches) and report the median or mean over repeats with fixed prompt, batch and lengths.

selfTest.q: The cached run is faster but its tokens differ from the baseline. Is that a valid speedup?
selfTest.a: No. Verify identical tokens or logits first at a fixed seed. Different outputs mean different work or a correctness bug, so fix that before claiming anything.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook 23 Sections 2 and 3: acceptance and exactness
study.locator: Section 2 (draft guesses \(K\) tokens, target verifies in one pass) and Section 3 (accept_prob as \(\min(1, p_{\text{target}}/p_{\text{draft}})\)) with Exercise 1 (0.5 versus 0.8 giving 1.0)
study.depth: Do Sections 2 and 3 and Exercise 1 only. Skip Exercises 2 and 3: their expected-token formula drops the extra token the target always contributes, so their numbers disagree with the \(K+1\) ceiling. Skip draft-model training and variants; they belong to later tracks.

focus: Sharing needs exact token equality on the prefix. One differing token ends sharing after that point, and only later blocks diverge.
Pages are fixed-size blocks with a table from logical to physical positions. Waste per sequence caps at \(\text{block}_{\text{size}}-1\) instead of \(\text{max}_{\text{len}}-1\).
Forks share prefix pages and copy on write. Only the diverged block is copied, not the whole prefix.
Speculation is exact: the acceptance ratio plus the residual correction reproduce target-only sampling. Speed depends on draft quality, not on luck.
units.reproduce: Draw the shared-prefix block table for two requests over an 8-token prefix with block_size 4, show the copy-on-write step on divergence, and state the speculative exactness contract with the acceptance formula.
traps: Treating speculative decoding as approximate sampling. Unverified draft tokens change the distribution; only the accept plus correction loop preserves it.
Expecting sharing across different prefixes. Similar text with different token ids shares nothing; the match is on tokens, not meaning.
Paging away the math. Blocks only relocate storage; attention still gathers the same \(K\) and \(V\), so outputs must match contiguous storage exactly.

selfTest.q: Two requests share an 8-token system prefix with block_size 4. How many physical prefix blocks with sharing versus without?
selfTest.a: 2 shared blocks versus 4 (2 per request). Sharing saves half the prefix memory, and a divergence copies only the affected block.

selfTest.q: Draft assigns token \(A\) 0.5 and target assigns 0.8. What is the acceptance probability?
selfTest.a: \(\min(1, 0.8/0.5)=1.0\), so always accept.

selfTest.q: A draft proposes \(K=4\) tokens and each is accepted with probability 0.5, independently. How many tokens does one target pass yield on average, and what is the ceiling?
selfTest.a: \((1-0.5^5)/(1-0.5)=1.94\), counting the token the target always adds after the last accepted draft token. A perfect draft gives \(K+1=5\). Notebook 23's exercises use \(1-\alpha^K\) and drop that token, so trust the \(K+1\) form.

selfTest.q: Does speculative decoding change the output distribution?
selfTest.a: No. With the residual correction it is exact and equals target-only sampling. It changes speed, not the distribution.
